title: The Book of Proverbs
lead: The book of Proverbs, Israel's main collection of wisdom sayings and teaching speeches, with the proverbs found elsewhere in the Bible: how the collections were made, how they relate to the wisdom of Egypt and Mesopotamia, and how Jews and Christians have read them.

sections.h: Proverbs outside the book of Proverbs
sections.b: Israel quoted proverbs long before the book was gathered. Popular sayings appear in the stories: "A hero of the hunt in the LORD's sight, like Nimrod" (Genesis 10:9), "Is Saul among the prophets too?" (1 Samuel 10:12; compare 1 Samuel 19:24), "Out of the wicked comes wickedness" (1 Samuel 24:13), and the sour-grapes saying that both Jeremiah and Ezekiel reject (Jeremiah 31:29; Ezekiel 18:2). The Hebrew word mashal covers all of these, and also a taunt song (Isaiah 14:4) and a parable (Ezekiel 17:2). Solomon is said to have spoken three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 4:32). Ecclesiastes and Job use and test the same kind of saying, and Sirach, written about 180 BC, continues the tradition in Hebrew. In the New Testament, Jesus' teaching is full of proverb-shaped sayings, and James is often called the New Testament's wisdom book.

sections.b: Proverbs names its own parts. "The proverbs of Solomon" (1:1) open the father's talks and Wisdom's speeches of chapters 1–9. A second heading, "The proverbs of Solomon" (10:1), begins about 375 two-line sayings (10:1–22:16). "The words of the wise" (22:17–24:22) and "These too are sayings of the wise" (24:23–34) follow, then the proverbs "the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied" (25:1–29:27), the words of Agur (30) and the words of Lemuel, taught him by his mother (31:1–9), and the poem of the woman of strength (31:10–31). Most scholars think chapters 1–9 and 31:10–31 were set around the older collections last, perhaps in the Persian period, as a frame for reading them.
